title: The Beast from the Sea and the Beast from the Earth
summary: The dragon calls up a beast from the sea with ten horns and seven heads, one of which recovers from a mortal wound; the world marvels, worships the dragon and the beast, and the beast makes war on the saints for 42 months. A second beast rises from the earth, looking like a lamb but speaking like a dragon, and makes people worship the first beast through signs, a speaking image, and a mark without which no one can buy or sell. The chapter ends with a call for wisdom: the number of the beast is the number of a man, 666.
story: Chapter 12 ended with the dragon standing on the seashore, enraged and determined to make war on the woman's children. Now he finds his instruments. The first beast is political power claiming worship; the second is the religious and social machinery that persuades people to give it. Together with the dragon they form a counterfeit of God, the Lamb, and the Spirit. This is the most direct portrait in the book of what the churches faced when loyalty to Jesus collided with the demands of empire, and it sets the terms for chapter 14, which answers it with the Lamb on Mount Zion and the warning against taking the beast's mark.
historical:
For readers in Asia, the beast rising from the sea would have looked a great deal like Rome, whose governors and power arrived from across the sea in the west. Revelation 17:9 later ties its seven heads to seven hills, and Rome was famous as the city on seven hills. The mortal wound that was healed has been read against the events of AD 68 to 69: Nero took his own life in 68, the empire fell into civil war as four emperors ruled in a single year, and then stabilized under Vespasian. Roman historians (Tacitus and Suetonius among them) also report a widespread rumor that Nero had not really died and would return from the east, and more than one pretender claiming to be Nero appeared in the following years. Many interpreters think the healed head plays on that rumor.

The second beast fits the institutions that promoted emperor worship in Asia: local elites and priests who built temples, organized festivals, and set up images of the emperor, with the province's cities competing for the honor. Trade guilds, through which many people earned their living, held banquets under the patronage of gods, and refusing to take part could cost a believer customers and standing (compare 2:14, 20). The Greek word for mark was used for the official stamp on documents and for the image impressed on coins, which bore the emperor's likeness and titles.
cultural:
The first beast is a composite of the four beasts that rise from the sea in Daniel 7: the lion, the bear, the leopard, and a fourth beast with ten horns. John's single beast gathers all the empires of Daniel into one, and like Daniel's little horn it speaks arrogant words and wars against the holy ones for a time, times, and half a time (Daniel 7:8, 21, 25). The image that people are made to worship recalls Nebuchadnezzar's golden statue in Daniel 3, which all had to bow to on pain of death. The second beast calls down fire from heaven, as Elijah did (1 Kings 18:38), a counterfeit of true prophecy; Jesus warned that false prophets would perform signs to deceive (Mark 13:22), and Revelation later calls this beast the false prophet (16:13).

The mark on the right hand or forehead is the counterpart of two other markings. God's servants have been sealed on their foreheads (7:3), and Israel was told to bind God's commands on the hand and between the eyes (Deuteronomy 6:8). The mark shows whose you are and what governs your thinking and doing. Ancient languages used letters as numbers, and adding up the letters of a name (called gematria) was common: a wall scratching at Pompeii reads, in Greek, that the writer loves a woman whose number is 545.
literary: The chapter is a deliberate parody of what has come before. The dragon gives the beast “his power and his throne and great authority”, as God gives the Lamb his throne. The beast's head appears to have been mortally wounded, using the same word used for the Lamb who appeared to have been slain (5:6). The world's cry, “Who is like the beast?”, mimics the Old Testament's praise, Who is like the LORD (Exodus 15:11). The second beast has horns like a lamb. The repeated verb was given or was permitted (vv. 5, 7, 14, 15) reminds the reader that even the beast acts only within limits God allows, for 42 months. Two interruptions address the hearers directly, in the style of the seven letters: “He who has an ear, let him hear” (v. 9), with a call for perseverance and faith (v. 10), and a call for wisdom and insight (v. 18).

outline.t: The beast from the sea and its healed wound
The beast blasphemes and wars on the saints
A call for perseverance and faith
The beast from the earth and the speaking image
The mark of the beast and the number 666

doctrines.note: The beast demands worship, and the world gives it, marveling at power and asking who can fight it. Revelation shows that idolatry is not only about statues: it is giving to any human power the trust and allegiance that belong to God alone.

Verse 10 answers the beast's power with “the perseverance and faith of the saints.” Faith here is steady faithfulness, refusing both violent resistance and compromise, and trusting God with the outcome.

The beast is repeatedly given and permitted what it does, and only for a set time. Those who belong to God are written in the Lamb's Book of Life. Evil is real and wounds the saints, but it does not rule the story.
The chapter calls for wisdom and insight to recognize the beast. Biblical wisdom here is spiritual discernment: seeing through power that disguises itself as a lamb.

words.note: Thērion, a wild animal, a beast. Where Christ is the Lamb, the powers opposed to God are beasts, violent and devouring, following Daniel 7. The word appears sixteen times in this chapter, dominating it as the throne dominated chapter 4.

Charagma, a mark, stamp, or engraved image. It was used for the imprint on coins and seals and for official stamps. In Revelation it marks allegiance to the beast, the counterpart of God's seal on his servants' foreheads; both mark whom a person belongs to.

Psēphizō, to calculate, literally to count with pebbles. It tells the hearer that the number can be worked out by those with insight, which is why most interpreters think John expected his first readers to be able to decode it.

Hupomonē, perseverance, patient endurance, literally remaining under a load. John calls himself a partner in it (1:9). In the face of the beast, the saints' response is neither violence nor surrender but faithful endurance.

christ: Christ is present in this chapter chiefly by contrast. The beast's healed wound parodies the Lamb who was slain and lives; the second beast has horns like a lamb but speaks like the dragon. The world asks who is like the beast, and the book's answer is the Lamb, whose power is self-giving rather than devouring. Those who refuse the beast are those whose names are written in the Book of Life of the Lamb who was slain. The word for this pattern in the New Testament is antichrist, a counterfeit that imitates Christ's form while opposing his way (1 John 2:18-22). The chapter also calls believers to follow Jesus' own path: he refused the devil's offer of the world's kingdoms in exchange for worship (Matthew 4:8-10), and he endured rather than took up the sword (Matthew 26:52, which verse 10's sayings on captivity and the sword recall, along with Jeremiah 15:2).

hard.q: Who is the beast, and what does 666 mean?
hard.a:
The main readings deserve to be stated fairly. Many interpreters, especially preterists, think John meant Nero. Letters in Hebrew and Greek also served as numbers, and the Greek title Nerōn Kaisar written in Hebrew letters (a spelling found in an Aramaic document of the period) adds up to 666. Some early manuscripts, including a papyrus fragment found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt and one of the major fifth-century codices, read 616 instead, and Irenaeus in the late second century knew copies with that number. The Latin form Nero Caesar, without the final n, adds up to 616 in Hebrew letters, which would explain the variant neatly. Irenaeus himself, however, preferred 666 and discussed several possible names without settling on one. Others read 666 symbolically: six falls short of seven, the number of completeness, so 666 is imperfection tripled, a human power that always falls short of the divine it claims to be; some note that the Greek name Jesus adds up to 888. Some connect it with Solomon's annual income of 666 talents of gold (1 Kings 10:14), the moment Israel's king began to trust in wealth. Historicists of the Reformation era identified the beast with the papacy; futurists generally expect a final individual ruler, the antichrist, still to come; idealists see the beast as a recurring pattern of state power demanding worship in every age.

These readings are not all exclusive: John may have pointed his first readers to a figure they knew while describing a pattern that recurs and culminates at the end. Christian history is littered with confident identifications of the beast with figures of the reader's own day, and all of them were wrong. The chapter's call is not to speculation but to wisdom and endurance: to recognize any power that demands the worship due to God, and to refuse it.

questions: The beast's power makes the world marvel and ask who can fight it. What forms of power are you most tempted to admire or fear?
The mark decides who can buy and sell. Where does faithfulness to Christ cost, or might cost, you economically or socially?
The second beast looks like a lamb but speaks like a dragon. How can believers learn to tell the difference between true and counterfeit faith in public life?
